meta.blurb: Sam is forty-two and loses his breath chasing a football. His eight-year-old daughter runs for pure joy, so he decides to learn again, one gentle step at a time, from a first slow jog to a first five-kilometre run.
meta.bible: Sam: a forty-two-year-old office worker who has not run since school, cheerful and a little stubborn. Joy: his eight-year-old daughter, who runs everywhere for fun. Ana: a volunteer running coach in her fifties, calm and funny, who leads a Saturday morning beginners group in Elm Park. Maria: a sixty-eight-year-old club runner and a friend of Ana. The story lasts twelve weeks and ends with a fun run of five kilometres in the town. Key ideas: walk-run, the talk test, easy pace, short quick steps, rest days, strength work, doing too much too soon, runner's high, warm-up, taper. The science is real and hedged: scientists think humans may be well built for long-distance running but this is debated; research on shoes, stretching and the ten percent rule is mixed; no invented numbers or studies. Anyone with a health condition should speak to a doctor before starting. Voice: warm, encouraging, practical, never pushy. This book is general information and is not medical advice.

beats.scene: Sam bends over, out of breath, while his daughter runs on with a ball
beats.summary: Sam is out of breath after a short sprint, while his daughter Joy runs on easily.

beats.scene: Joy runs in circles across the grass, arms wide and laughing
beats.summary: Joy runs for no reason except joy, and Sam wonders what she knows that he has forgotten.

beats.scene: Sam sits on a bench and looks at an old school running medal
beats.summary: Sam remembers that he loved running as a boy and decides to try again.

beats.scene: A woman in a bright jacket greets a small group in a park
beats.summary: Sam joins a Saturday beginners group in Elm Park and meets the coach, Ana.

beats.scene: Ana raises a hand and points to a health sign beside the group
beats.summary: Ana says that anyone with a health condition should talk to a doctor before starting to run.

beats.scene: Ana draws a tall running figure with long legs on a whiteboard
beats.summary: Ana says scientists think the human body may be well built for running long distances.

beats.scene: A sweating runner on a hot day beside a panting dog in the shade
beats.summary: Humans cool down by sweating over most of the skin, which may help them keep going in heat.

beats.scene: A drawing of a foot and heel with a spring beside it
beats.summary: The Achilles tendon and the arch of the foot work like springs that return energy with each step.

beats.scene: A runner seen from behind with large leg muscles and an upright back
beats.summary: Strong buttock muscles help keep the upper body steady and upright while running.

beats.scene: Early hunters walk across a hot plain after a distant antelope
beats.summary: Some scientists suggest early humans may have chased animals until the animals were exhausted, but this is debated.

beats.scene: The group stands in a circle in the park while Ana waves her arms
beats.summary: Ana says that whatever the past was, a body trained gently can learn to run, and starting small is the key.

beats.scene: Sam holds up a pair of plain running shoes in a shop
beats.summary: Ana says a comfortable, well-fitting shoe is enough and that research on expensive shoes is mixed.

beats.scene: A pair of bare feet running on a grassy path at the park edge
beats.summary: Some people like barefoot running, but the science is not settled and anyone trying it should go very slowly.

beats.scene: The group jogs gently and then walks along the park path in a line
beats.summary: The first session uses a walk-run plan: one minute of gentle jogging, then two minutes of walking.

beats.scene: Two runners chat while jogging side by side along a tree-lined path
beats.summary: The talk test: you should be able to speak in short sentences while you run, and that tells you your pace is right.

beats.scene: Sam leans forward with a red face and open mouth while others pass calmly
beats.summary: Sam starts too fast and gasps, and Ana tells him to go slower than he thinks he should.

beats.scene: A runner breathes out in a cold morning, with a small cloud of breath
beats.summary: There is no special breathing method; breathe in whatever way feels natural, through the nose, the mouth or both.

beats.scene: A relaxed runner stands tall with eyes on the horizon and loose shoulders
beats.summary: Good posture means standing tall, relaxing the shoulders and looking ahead rather than down.

beats.scene: Feet landing close under a runner's body, with short quick steps
beats.summary: Short, quick steps that land under the body are usually easier on the legs than long, reaching strides.

beats.scene: A runner's arms swing gently with relaxed loose hands
beats.summary: The arms should swing loosely, with relaxed hands, as if holding a bag of crisps without crushing it.

beats.scene: Sam walks stiffly down the stairs while holding the handrail and wincing
beats.summary: Mild muscle soreness after a first run is normal, but sharp pain is a signal to stop.

beats.scene: Sam rests on a sofa with his feet up while Joy brings water
beats.summary: Rest days matter, because the body grows stronger during rest; beginners should run every other day.

beats.scene: Sam and Joy run side by side along the path with Joy skipping ahead
beats.summary: In the second week Joy joins Sam, and he sees how children treat running as a game.

beats.scene: Sam and Joy race to a lamp post, then walk laughing
beats.summary: Playing with speed, such as racing to a lamp post, makes training fun and teaches the body to change pace.

beats.scene: A runner drinks from a small bottle on a park bench in the sun
beats.summary: For short runs most people only need to drink when thirsty; there is no need to force down large amounts.

beats.scene: A bowl of porridge and a banana on a table in the morning light
beats.summary: Normal meals are enough for beginners; a small snack can help, but a big meal just before running is a bad idea.

beats.scene: Sam rubs his sore knee, sitting on a bench beside the path
beats.summary: In week three Sam's knee starts to ache, and Ana tells him to stop, rest and see a doctor or physiotherapist if it persists.

beats.scene: A line drawing of a steadily rising staircase beside a runner's feet
beats.summary: Most running injuries come from doing too much too soon; the ten percent rule is only a rough guide.

beats.scene: Sam does a squat in the living room while Joy counts and copies him
beats.summary: Simple strength exercises such as squats, calf raises and planks twice a week may help runners avoid injuries.

beats.scene: A runner walks briskly and swings their legs gently before a run
beats.summary: A warm-up of brisk walking and easy movements is a good start; the evidence for stretching before a run is mixed.

beats.scene: Sam sleeps deeply in bed while the moon shines through the window
beats.summary: Good sleep helps the body recover from running, and tired legs often need more sleep, not more miles.

beats.scene: A heart drawn inside a runner's chest with arrows showing blood moving
beats.summary: Regular running trains the heart to pump more blood with each beat, and the resting heart rate may fall.

beats.scene: A strong bone and joint drawn with small arrows showing gentle pressure
beats.summary: Running puts gentle load on bones and joints, which can make bones stronger; studies have generally not found that recreational running wears out knees.

beats.scene: A smiling runner at sunrise with arms spread wide on a hill
beats.summary: Some runners feel a happy lift called runner's high, but scientists are still unsure why, and not everyone feels it.

beats.scene: Rain falls on an empty park path while Sam looks out of a window
beats.summary: On a rainy day without motivation Ana advises making the task small: put on the shoes and go out for ten minutes.

beats.scene: A runner in a bright jacket runs through rain, sun and snow
beats.summary: Dress for the weather in layers, slow down in the heat, and wear bright colours in poor light.

beats.scene: A runner on a pavement faces oncoming traffic with a phone in a pocket
beats.summary: Safety: run facing traffic, tell someone where you are going, carry a phone, and take care with headphones.

beats.scene: Sam jogs beside Maria, a smiling woman with grey hair, among other runners
beats.summary: Running with others makes it more fun, and Sam meets Maria, a sixty-eight-year-old club runner.

beats.scene: A group of runners walks up a green hill and runs down it again
beats.summary: On hills, walk the steep parts with short steps and take care going downhill.

beats.scene: Sam jogs along a path and checks a stopwatch while smiling with surprise
beats.summary: In week eight Sam runs for twenty minutes without stopping and is proud of himself.

beats.scene: Sam walks slowly and heavily along the path, hands on hips
beats.summary: Progress is not a straight line, and a heavy, slow day is normal and not a failure.

beats.scene: A group jogs easily while one runner speeds up for a short stretch
beats.summary: Most runs should be easy, with perhaps one slightly harder session a week.

beats.scene: Sam swims in a pool while Joy watches from the side with a towel
beats.summary: Other exercise such as swimming, cycling or walking gives the running muscles a rest and adds variety.

beats.scene: Joy sprints ahead and stops panting while Sam passes at a steady pace
beats.summary: Joy sprints too fast and tires, which teaches Sam the importance of pacing evenly.

beats.scene: Sam rests with a cup of tea beside a calendar with a circled date
beats.summary: In week eleven Sam eases off before the fun run, a practice called tapering, and rests and sleeps well.

beats.scene: Sam eats porridge in running clothes with a number pinned to his shirt
beats.summary: On race morning Sam eats a small, familiar breakfast and tries nothing new.

beats.scene: Runners of many ages and shapes wait behind a start line in a park
beats.summary: At the start, people of all ages and speeds wait together, and Sam learns that everyone's race is their own.

beats.scene: Sam runs with a determined face while Joy waves from the side
beats.summary: Near three kilometres the run gets hard, and Sam uses small tricks such as counting steps and thinking of Joy waiting at the end.

beats.scene: Sam and Joy cross the finish line together with their arms in the air
beats.summary: Sam finishes the five kilometres with Joy beside him, and his time does not matter.

beats.scene: Ana and Sam sit on the grass at sunset with Joy asleep nearby
beats.summary: Ana ends by saying: keep running gently, listen to your body, and remember that this book is general information and not medical advice.

B1B2: Sam is forty-two, and he has just run twenty steps after a football. He is gasping for air, while his daughter Joy is still racing happily across the grass.
Joy does not run to burn calories or to win a medal. She runs because it feels good, and she cannot imagine a reason not to.
That evening, Sam finds an old school medal in a drawer and remembers racing his friends at lunch. He decides that he wants to run again, even if it is slowly.
The next Saturday, Sam joins a beginners group in Elm Park, led by a volunteer coach named Ana. She smiles at everyone and says that nobody in this group is too slow.
Before they begin, Ana gives one important piece of advice. If you have a health problem, or if you are unsure, you should talk to your doctor before you start.
Ana tells the group that some scientists believe humans are built to run long distances. She says this idea is still debated, but the clues are interesting.
Many animals cool down by panting, but humans have sweat glands all over the skin. This may help us keep going in the heat, when other animals must stop and rest.
Behind your ankle, the thick Achilles tendon stretches and then springs back with every step. Together with the arch of the foot, it returns some of the energy you spend.
The big muscles in your buttocks may look unimportant, but they work hard when you run. They keep your upper body steady, so that you do not fall forward with every step.
Some scientists suggest that early humans may have followed animals for hours in the heat, until the animals were too tired to run. Others are not sure, and nobody can go back to check.
Ana says that you do not have to believe any theory about the past to start running. If you begin small and build slowly, most healthy bodies will gradually learn to enjoy it.
Sam asks Ana which running shoes he should buy. She tells him to choose a pair that fits well and feels comfortable, because the research on expensive shoes is mixed.
Joy asks if she can run barefoot like the grass-loving children she sees. Ana says that some adults enjoy it too, but the evidence is unclear, and anyone who tries it should go very slowly.
The first session is a mix of walking and jogging. They jog for one minute, then walk for two, and they repeat this several times.
Ana teaches the group something she calls the talk test. If you can say a few sentences while you run, your pace is about right, and if you cannot, you should slow down.
Sam starts the first jog too quickly and is soon red in the face. Ana jogs beside him and tells him to go slower than he thinks he needs to.
Sam wonders if there is a secret way to breathe while running. Ana says that there is not, and that he can breathe through his nose, his mouth or both.
Ana shows the group a simple way to hold the body. Stand tall, let the shoulders drop, and look at the path ahead instead of at your feet.
Many beginners take steps that are too long, which makes each landing harder on the legs. Ana suggests short, quick steps, with the foot landing under the body.
Ana tells the group to bend the elbows and swing the arms gently forward and back. She says the hands should be loose, as if holding a packet of crisps without crushing it.
The next morning, Sam can hardly walk down the stairs because his legs are so sore. Ana says that mild soreness is normal, but that a sharp pain is a signal to stop.
Ana explains that a body does not become stronger during the run itself. It gets stronger afterwards, while it rests, so beginners should run on every other day.
In the second week, Joy asks if she can run with her father. She skips ahead, runs back, and turns every straight path into a game.
Joy shouts that she will race him to the next lamp post. Sam laughs, speeds up for a few seconds, and then slows down again, and he discovers that playing with speed is fun.
Sam asks how much water he should drink on a run. Ana says that for a short run, most people only need to drink when they feel thirsty.
Ana says that beginners do not need special food. Normal meals are enough, and a small snack an hour before running is fine, but a big meal just before is not a good idea.
In the third week, Sam feels a sharp ache in his knee, and he stops at once. Ana tells him to rest, and to see a doctor or physiotherapist if the pain does not go away.
Ana says that many running injuries come from doing too much, too soon. There is an old rule of adding no more than ten percent a week, but it is only a rough guide.
While his knee rests, Sam learns some simple strength exercises. He does squats, calf raises and planks twice a week, which may help to protect runners from injuries.
Ana advises a warm-up before each run, such as brisk walking and gentle leg swings. Evidence for long stretching before running is mixed, so she keeps this part short and easy.
Sam notices that on the nights after a run, he sleeps more deeply. Ana says that sleep is when the body recovers, so tired legs need more sleep, not more running.
Ana explains that the heart is a muscle, and that regular running trains it. Over time it can pump more blood with each beat, and the resting heart rate may become lower.
Sam asks Ana whether running will ruin his knees for good. She says that studies have generally not found that recreational runners have worse knees, and that the gentle load can make bones stronger.
Some runners feel a burst of happiness during or after a run, often called a runner's high. Scientists are still unsure what causes it, and not everyone feels it.
One rainy morning, Sam would much rather stay in bed. He remembers Ana's advice to make the task small, so he puts on his shoes and promises himself ten minutes.
Ana says that the right clothes make every season easier. Wear thin layers that you can remove, slow down on hot days, and choose bright colours when the light is poor.
Before they set off, Ana gives the group some simple safety rules. Tell someone where you are going, carry a phone, face the traffic when there is no pavement, and keep any headphones quiet.
At the club, Sam meets Maria, who is sixty-eight and has been running for thirty years. She tells him that running with other people makes it easier to turn up when you do not feel like it.
Elm Park has a long hill that Sam has always been afraid of. Ana says that it is fine to walk the steep parts, with short steps, and to go carefully on the way down.
In the eighth week, Sam runs for twenty minutes without a single walking break. When he stops, his eyes are wet, because eight weeks ago he could not run for one.
In the ninth week, Sam has a terrible run, and his legs feel as if they are made of stone. Ana tells him that progress is never a straight line, and that heavy days happen to everybody.
Ana tells the group that most of their runs should be easy. Once a week they can try something a little harder, but the rest should be gentle, so that the body can recover.
On his rest days, Sam sometimes swims or rides a bicycle. Ana says that this kind of variety rests the muscles that run, and it keeps exercise fun.
Joy challenges Sam to a longer race, and she sprints off at top speed. She is soon out of breath, and Sam passes her at a steady pace, which teaches them both about pacing.
In the week before the fun run, Ana tells everyone to run a little less. This is called tapering, and it lets the legs rest so that they feel fresh on the day.
On the morning of the fun run, Sam is nervous, and his hands shake as he pins his number on. He eats a plain breakfast, because Ana has told him never to try anything new on the day.
At the start line, Sam sees runners of every age, shape and speed, from teenagers to grandparents. He realises that everyone is running their own race, and nobody is watching him.
Around the third kilometre, Sam's legs begin to ache and he wants to stop. He counts his steps, breathes slowly, and thinks of Joy waiting for him at the end.
Joy jumps over the barrier at the end and takes her father's hand. Together they cross the finish line, and Sam's time does not matter to either of them.

Ana tells Sam to keep running gently and to listen to his body, and she says goodbye with a smile. This book is general information only and is not medical advice, so please talk to a doctor about your own health.
C1C2: On a bright Saturday in the park, Sam chased a football for no more than twenty steps before his lungs began to burn. He bent over with his hands on his knees, wheezing like an old kettle, and wondered when his body had become so unfit. Ahead of him, his eight-year-old daughter Joy was still sprinting in wide circles, laughing as though she had never been tired in her life.

Nobody had ever taught Joy how to run, and nobody had to, because children seem to run the way birds sing. She ran to the swings, to the gate, to the lamp post and back again, simply for the pleasure of feeling the wind in her face. Sam watched her and felt a strange pang of envy, because he could no longer remember when running had last felt like that.

Later that evening, while searching a drawer for batteries, Sam found a tarnished school medal and, with it, a flood of memories of races on the playground at lunchtime. He had loved running once, long before desks, deadlines and the car had taken its place. By the time he closed the drawer, he had made up his mind to try again, however slowly and clumsily it might go.

At nine o'clock the following Saturday, Sam shuffled into Elm Park, where a small group of nervous strangers had gathered around a woman in a bright yellow jacket. Her name was Ana, she explained, and she had been coaching beginners for many years as a volunteer. Nobody here was too old, too heavy or too slow, she announced cheerfully, and Sam felt his shoulders drop for the first time that week.

Before anyone took a single step, Ana raised a hand and gave the one piece of advice she called non-negotiable. If you have a heart problem, an injury, a long-term illness or simply any doubt, she said, speak to your doctor before you start running. Sam had already checked with his own, and he was glad to hear it was a rule the whole group took seriously.

Humans are not fast, Ana told the group, because a cat, a horse or a hare would leave us far behind in a short sprint. Over long distances, however, some scientists believe our bodies have unusual strengths, though the idea is still debated and the evidence is not complete. Sam, who had always thought of himself as built for sitting, listened with growing curiosity.

Dogs and horses cool themselves by panting or by sweating in limited places, but a human being can sweat across almost the whole body. As the sweat dries on the skin, it carries heat away, which is a remarkable way to keep a hard-working body from overheating. Some researchers think this ability may help explain why people can keep moving on hot days when many animals must stop.

Ana asked the group to touch the thick cord behind their ankles, the Achilles tendon, and explained that it works rather like an elastic band. It stretches as the foot lands and then recoils as the body moves forward, returning part of the energy that would otherwise be lost. The arch of the foot does a similar job, so that every stride is partly powered by springs you already own.

Few people give any thought to the muscles of the buttocks, yet Ana called them the engine room of a runner. With each stride, they pull the leg back and hold the trunk upright, so that the body does not tip forward and crumple at every step. Chimpanzees, she added with a grin, have much smaller ones, and they would find our kind of running very difficult.

One famous idea holds that our ancestors hunted by following an animal across the open plain for hours, until the creature was too hot and weary to flee. Other researchers doubt that this was common, pointing out that the evidence is thin and that people probably used many methods. Ana said that the past did not matter much for the group, since the lesson for today was simply that running is a natural thing to do.

Whatever our ancestors did on the plains, Ana told the group, the point was that bodies adapt to the work we give them, provided we are patient. Muscles, bones, tendons and lungs all grow stronger a little at a time, but only when the load rises slowly enough for them to keep up. Starting small, she said, was not a sign of weakness but the secret that every experienced runner has learned.

Sam had spent an hour online reading about cushioning, carbon plates and stability, and he arrived on Saturday more confused than when he began. Ana laughed kindly and told him that the best shoe is one that fits well, feels comfortable and is not worn out. The research on special features is mixed, she said, and no single shoe has ever been proved right for everybody.

Joy kicked off her sandals and ran across the grass in her bare feet, and Sam asked whether he should do the same. Some runners swear by it, Ana said, while others have found that it hurt, and the science has not settled the question in either direction. If you want to try, she advised, begin with short distances on soft ground and let your feet and calves adapt very slowly.

Ana explained that the whole group would begin with a simple pattern that many beginners use, called walk-run. They would jog gently for one minute, then walk for two, and repeat the cycle until about twenty minutes had passed. To Sam's surprise, the walking breaks felt less like failure than like a clever way of sharing the effort across the morning.

Sam asked how fast a beginner ought to run, and Ana gave him a simple answer in the form of a game she called the talk test. You must be able to say a short sentence aloud without gasping, she explained, and that is all. If the words come out in broken pieces, she said, you are going too fast, and the cure is simply to slow down until a conversation becomes possible.

When the first whistle blew, Sam shot off along the path as if he were being chased, and within a minute his chest was heaving and his legs felt like wet sand. Ana jogged calmly alongside him and told him, with great gentleness, that his pace should feel almost embarrassingly slow. He tried again, and to his amazement he reached the end of the minute smiling instead of panting.

Sam had read that serious runners follow strict patterns of breathing, and he worried that he was doing it wrong. Ana reassured him that there was no magic method and that the best way to breathe is whichever feels natural, using the nose, the mouth, or both together. If his breath feels out of control, she added, the solution is almost always a slower pace.

Posture, Ana said, does not need to be perfect, but a few small habits make the run feel lighter. Imagine a string lifting you gently from the top of your head, let your shoulders drop away from your ears, and look at the path some distance ahead. Sam straightened up, and to his surprise his breathing felt a little easier at once.

Many beginners reach out with the front foot, as if they were trying to leap over a puddle, which makes each landing harder and slows the body down. Ana suggested shorter, quicker steps with the feet landing more nearly under the hips, although she was careful to say that the research on running form is not clear-cut. Sam tried it, and the whole stride began to feel lighter, like a quiet patter instead of a thump.

Tension, Ana explained, is a runner's silent thief, and it often hides in the fists and the shoulders. She told everyone to bend their elbows, swing their arms gently from front to back, and keep their hands as relaxed as if they were carrying a delicate egg. Sam looked down and found that he had been clenching his fists the whole morning.

Sam woke the next day with legs so stiff that he descended the stairs backwards, one painful step at a time, to the delight of his daughter. Ana had warned him that this dull ache, which lasts a day or two, is common when muscles are doing something new. A sharp, sudden or lasting pain, she had added, is a different matter, and a good reason to stop and seek advice.

It is a strange truth, Ana told the group, that you do not get fitter while you run but in the hours of recovery that follow. During the effort, you place a small stress on the body, and in the rest that follows the body rebuilds itself a little stronger than before. For that reason, beginners are wise to run only every second day, leaving the days in between for sleeping, walking and doing nothing at all.

By the second week, Joy had grown so curious about her father's new habit that she begged to come along. She treated the run as one great game, skipping ahead, circling back, jumping over cracks and inventing rules that changed with every lamp post. Sam realised that she had never once looked at a watch, and that she seemed to enjoy herself far more than he did.

Joy pointed at a lamp post a hundred steps ahead and challenged her father to a race, and Sam, to his own surprise, accepted. He sped up for a few joyful seconds, collapsed into a gentle jog, and found that his legs had enjoyed the sudden change. Ana later told him that this kind of playful variation, mixing short quick bursts with easy running, has a name among coaches, but that it began as nothing more than a children's game.

Sam turned up for his third session carrying a bottle the size of a small bucket, which made Ana smile. For a short run, she said, a normal person who has had a normal day only needs to drink when thirsty, and forcing down large amounts can do more harm than good. Longer runs in the heat call for more care, but that was a problem for another year.

Sam wondered whether he needed protein shakes, energy gels or some secret diet, but Ana laughed at the idea. A beginner who runs for twenty or thirty minutes does well with ordinary meals made of simple, varied food, perhaps with a small snack such as a banana an hour beforehand. A heavy meal just before a run, she warned, is a good recipe for a stitch.

In the third week, a sharp pain stabbed at the side of Sam's knee halfway through the run, and he stopped on the spot, cross with himself. Ana told him he had done exactly the right thing, because running through real pain can turn a small problem into a long one. She told him to rest for a few days, and to see a doctor or a physiotherapist if it did not settle.

Looking at Sam's knee, Ana said that the most common story among runners is a happy beginning that ends in an injury, because enthusiasm grows faster than the body's strength. Doing too much too soon is widely seen as one of the main causes. Coaches often quote a rule of adding no more than ten percent a week, but Ana called it a rough guide that has not been proved, and said that listening to the body matters more.

During his week of rest, Sam learned that a runner is not only a pair of legs, but a body that needs strength throughout. Ana showed him squats, calf raises and a plank, to be done twice a week at home, and said that research suggests strength work may help reduce running injuries. Joy copied every movement with great seriousness, and she was a much better plank than her father.

Before each session, Ana led the group through a short warm-up of brisk walking, gentle leg swings and a few easy knee lifts, so that the muscles were awake before the work began. Sam asked whether he should also stretch for a long time, and she answered that the evidence on stretching before exercise is mixed, and so she kept it brief. What mattered most, she said, was that you began slowly and let the body warm itself up.

Since he began running, Sam had noticed that he fell asleep faster and woke feeling more refreshed, although he was careful not to claim that this was scientific proof. Ana said that sleep is the time when the body repairs the small tears and strains of the day, and that people who skimp on it often feel tired during their runs. When your legs feel heavy, she told him, the right answer is often an earlier bedtime and not an extra mile.

The heart, Ana reminded the group, is a muscle like any other, and it grows stronger when it is asked to work regularly and gently. After weeks of steady training, it can push more blood around the body with each beat, which is why the resting heart rate of many regular runners becomes slower. Sam put two fingers on his wrist that evening and, to his delight, felt a calm, steady rhythm.

A neighbour had warned Sam that running would wreck his knees, and the worry had followed him around for weeks. Ana explained that bones respond to gentle pressure by becoming denser, and that studies of recreational runners have generally not found more knee arthritis than in people who do not run. Still, she said, individual bodies differ, and anyone with a joint problem should ask their doctor.

Halfway through his fifth week, Sam suddenly felt something like a warm glow spreading through his chest, a lightness that made the hill seem to flatten beneath him. Some runners call this a runner's high and have long linked it to chemicals in the brain, but researchers are still arguing about which chemicals matter and why. Not everyone experiences it, Ana said, and it is a pleasant bonus instead of a goal.

On the sixth Saturday, the sky was grey, rain was tapping at the window, and every sensible part of Sam wanted to stay in bed. Ana had warned him that motivation comes and goes, so she had taught him a trick of making the task so small that it is impossible to refuse, which meant putting on his shoes and going out for ten minutes. Twenty minutes later he was still plodding happily along the path, soaked to the skin, grinning like a fool, and quietly delighted that he had not given in.

Weather is no reason to stop, Ana told the group, but it does call for a little thought. On cold days, a few thin layers are better than one thick coat, because you can take one off as you warm up, while in summer it is wise to run in the shade and slow down. When the light is poor, she added, bright or reflective clothes help drivers to notice you from a safe distance.

Safety, Ana said, is the dullest part of running and the one that matters most. Tell somebody where you are going and when you will be back, carry a phone, run on a pavement where you can, and keep the volume of your headphones low enough to hear a car or a bicycle bell. If there is no pavement, she added, run facing the oncoming traffic so that you can see what is coming.

Sam found that the Saturday group was made up of an unlikely mix of ages, shapes and speeds, from students to grandparents. One of them, Maria, was sixty-eight years old and had been running for thirty years, and she jogged beside Sam and chatted all the way round the park. Having someone to meet, she said, makes it much easier to turn up on days when the sofa is calling.

At the far side of Elm Park there was a steady hill, and Sam eyed it as if it were a mountain. Ana told him that nobody expects a beginner to run up it, so he should shorten his steps, lean forward slightly and walk the steepest part with no shame whatever. Going downhill, she added, calls for care, since the legs absorb more force, and a controlled, relaxed stride is better than a rush.

In the eighth week, Sam looked at his watch, saw that twenty minutes had passed, and realised with a jolt that he had not walked once. Eight weeks earlier, he had been wheezing after twenty steps, and now he was jogging along contentedly with the sun on his back. When he finally stopped, he wiped his eyes and told Ana that it must be the wind.

In the ninth week, Sam had a terrible run, in which his legs felt like lead, every hill looked like a wall, and he wondered whether his earlier progress had been an illusion. Ana was entirely unworried and told him that improvement is never a straight line, that a bad day is usually caused by poor sleep, stress or tired muscles, and that even Olympic runners suffer from them. Two days later, after a good night's sleep and a day of complete rest, he ran as lightly as a deer and wondered what had worried him.

Ana explained that the surprising secret of many successful runners is that they run slowly most of the time, which leaves their legs fresh for the occasional harder effort. For the group, she suggested that most sessions should be easy and conversational, with perhaps one livelier session each week in which they pick up the pace for short stretches. The rest of the secret, she said with a smile, was simply patience, which no shop in the world is able to sell.

Sam found that a rest day did not have to mean doing nothing, and on one of them he took Joy swimming at the local pool. Ana encouraged this kind of variety, which coaches call cross-training, because swimming, cycling and brisk walking can build fitness while giving the running muscles a break. It also, she said, protects you from becoming bored, which is a quiet danger for anyone who wants to keep a habit for years.

Joy challenged her father to run all the way around the park, and she shot away at such speed that she looked like a rocket. Within three minutes she was bent over beside a bench, gasping, as Sam passed her at his slow and steady pace, and she could not help laughing at herself. The lesson, he told her kindly, is that the beginning of a long run should always feel too easy.

The week before the fun run, Ana made an announcement that astonished the beginners, which was that they should now run less. This practice, known as tapering, gives the muscles time to recover fully from weeks of training, so that the legs feel fresh and eager on the day itself. Sam obeyed, though he found it harder to rest than to run, and he spent the week watching the calendar.

On the morning of the fun run, Sam woke before the alarm with a stomach full of butterflies and a number to pin on his shirt. Ana had given him one golden rule, which was to try nothing new on race day, so he put on his usual shoes, ate his usual porridge and drank his usual tea. It all felt oddly ordinary for such a big day, and that, he realised as he laced his shoes, was exactly the whole point.

At the start line, hundreds of people shuffled and stretched together, including teenagers in bright shorts, grandparents in woolly hats and a man dressed as a banana. Sam had feared that he would be the slowest person there, but a glance around the crowd made him realise that everyone was running their own private race against their own private worries. Joy squeezed his hand tightly, he squeezed it back, and a moment later the whistle blew and the whole crowd surged gently forward.

Around the three-kilometre mark, the cheerful chatter of the start was replaced by the sound of laboured breathing, and Sam's legs began to scream for a rest. He did what Ana had taught him, counting his steps in fours, relaxing his shoulders and thinking only of the next lamp post rather than the distance still to go. Somewhere ahead, past the bend and the last of the trees, he knew that Joy would be waiting for him.

In the last two hundred metres, Joy jumped over the barrier, took her father's hand and dragged him towards the finish line, shouting that he must run faster. They crossed it together, with their arms in the air and their faces wet with sweat and laughter, and a volunteer hung a medal around Sam's neck. His time, he later discovered, was nothing to boast about, but he did not care at all.

Afterwards, Ana sat with Sam on the grass and told him that the real finish line had been the day he first put on his shoes, and that every run from now on was a bonus. This book has offered only general information, and it is not medical advice, so it cannot replace a conversation with a doctor or physiotherapist who knows your own body and history. Run gently, listen carefully to yourself, and remember what Joy knew all along, which is that running should be a joy.
